criteria.descriptor: Full marks: shadow vs canary mechanics are stated correctly (shadow = mirrored copy, output logged not served; canary = small % of real users actually served v2); guardrail metrics named are real and appropriate; rollback is described as a flag flip to a warm v1 rather than a redeploy; side-effect suppression and doubled cost of shadow are handled correctly. Deduct for any mechanism error (e.g. shadow serving responses, canary being offline).

Full marks: covers both stages in the right order, includes BOTH technical and quality/business guardrails, a staged canary ramp with bake time and control cohort, concrete rollback triggers, and explicitly answers the 'what shadow cannot tell you' ask. Partial credit if one of these elements (e.g. quality metrics, or the shadow-limitation answer) is missing.

Full marks: justifies WHY shadow precedes canary (de-risk stability/latency/cost with zero user exposure, then measure real impact), ties metric choices to this triage system, and explains why shadow's discarded output caps what it can validate. Lower marks for an unjustified checklist of steps.

Full marks: clear staged structure, correct use of terms (shadow/traffic mirroring, canary, guardrail metric, bake time, sticky sessions, rollback), and unambiguous thresholds/triggers. Lower marks for muddled ordering or vague, hand-wavy metrics.

expected_answer_points: Correctly distinguishes the mechanisms: shadow mirrors a copy of live traffic to v2 whose output is logged/compared but NOT served, while canary actually serves v2 to a small percentage of real users.
Sequences shadow first and justifies it: catches crashes/exceptions, malformed outputs, real-traffic p95/p99 latency and throughput, and cost/token usage before any user is exposed.
Then ramps canary in stages (e.g. 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with a bake period per stage and a v1 control cohort for comparison.
Defines concrete technical guardrails: p95/p99 latency, error/timeout (5xx) rate, and cost/tokens per request.

Defines quality guardrails appropriate to triage: agreement-with-v1 or delayed-label macro-F1 in shadow; human re-route/correction rate, draft acceptance/edit rate, and escalation/complaint rate in canary.
Specifies fast rollback via feature-flag flip to a warm v1 (config change, not redeploy), with explicit breach thresholds driving automated rollback plus a manual kill switch.
Names the key shadow limitation: it cannot measure real user/business quality because users never act on v2's output; that requires canary or delayed labels.
Flags shadow side-effect hazards: suppress duplicate user-facing actions (sending the drafted email), DB writes and downstream calls, and account for roughly doubled inference cost.
common_pitfalls: Conflates the two techniques - describes shadow as serving v2 to a subset of users, or thinks canary runs offline without real user exposure.
Claims shadow mode can validate user-facing or business quality (e.g. reply acceptance, resolution rate), when users never see v2's output so that signal is impossible from shadow alone.

Forgets that shadow duplicates side effects - fails to stub the drafted reply so it double-sends emails, double-writes to the DB, or double-charges the LLM API, and ignores the doubled inference cost.
Proposes rollback by rebuilding/redeploying v1 instead of an instant flag flip to a warm instance, or never keeps v1 warm, making recovery slow.
Lists only technical guardrails (latency, errors) with no quality/business metrics, or gives metrics with no concrete thresholds, bake time, or automated-rollback wiring.
Ignores sticky sessions and sample-size/significance in the canary, so users flip between v1 and v2 or conclusions are drawn from too little traffic.
reference_answer:
Run the rollout in two stages behind the traffic-routing / feature-flag layer, keeping v1 as the always-warm default so rollback is instant.

Stage 1 - Shadow (traffic mirroring / dark launch). Send a copy of every live request to v2 in parallel with v1, but keep serving v1's category and draft to users; v2's output is only logged and compared. This exercises v2 on the real input distribution and catches what offline eval cannot: crashes/exceptions, malformed or schema-invalid outputs, p95/p99 latency and throughput under production load, and token/cost per request. I would track agreement rate vs v1 and, where delayed ground truth exists (the category an agent ultimately routed to), v2's macro-F1 on live traffic. Critically, side effects must be suppressed - the shadow draft must never actually be sent, and DB writes / downstream API calls stubbed - and I would budget for roughly double inference cost while shadowing.

Stage 2 - Canary. Once v2 is stable in shadow, actually serve it to a small, sticky slice of real traffic - e.g. 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% - with a bake period at each step, comparing the canary cohort against a v1 control. Only now can I measure user-facing quality: human re-route/correction rate, draft acceptance / edit-distance, and escalation/complaint rate, alongside the technical guardrails.

Guardrails and rollback. Wire explicit thresholds - error/timeout rate, p95 latency, cost per request, and misroute rate relative to control - to automated rollback plus a manual kill switch. Rollback is a flag flip routing 100% back to the warm v1 (a config change, not a redeploy), so recovery is seconds.

Key limitation of shadow: because users never act on v2's output, shadow cannot tell you whether v2 is actually better for users/business - only that it runs and roughly agrees with v1. That verdict requires canary (or reliable delayed labels).
